NOTICE OF DEFAULT / NONJUDICIAL FORECLOSURE PROCESS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — INFORMATIONAL ONLY
This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's statutory process for a nonjudicial ("power of sale") foreclosure of a deed of trust under California Civil Code §§ 2924 et seq. — the process used for the large majority of California residential mortgage foreclosures. It concerns a loan affecting the real property commonly known as 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, secured by a deed of trust naming Pat Morgan as trustor (borrower) and Example Mortgage Lending, Inc. as beneficiary (lender). This sheet is informational only. It does not itself record, rescind, or otherwise affect any notice of default or notice of sale; it does not initiate, accelerate, halt, postpone, or complete any foreclosure of this or any other property; and it does not determine whether any actual default, notice, recording, posting, publication, or sale relating to this loan has complied — or failed to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes. Only the party or parties actually entitled to exercise the power of sale, acting through the statutory notice-and-waiting process described here, can begin or carry a nonjudicial foreclosure forward; only an actual reinstatement payment, payoff, or court order can stop one already begun.

POWER-OF-SALE (NONJUDICIAL) FORECLOSURE DISTINGUISHED FROM JUDICIAL FORECLOSURE
A deed of trust encumbering 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 may contain a "power of sale" clause — a private contractual grant of authority, running from Pat Morgan to a trustee, to sell the property after a default without first suing in court. California Civil Code § 2924(a) itself frames the power-of-sale mechanism this way: once "a power of sale is conferred upon the mortgagee, trustee, or any other person, to be exercised after a breach of the obligation for which that mortgage or transfer is a security," the statutory notice-and-waiting sequence described in this document is what governs how that power may actually be exercised. This is a fundamentally different mechanism from a judicial foreclosure, in which a lender files a lawsuit and a court enters a judgment or decree of foreclosure and orders the property sold — Section 2924(a) itself carves out, as a separate category, a transfer "made pursuant to an order, judgment, or decree of a court of record." A nonjudicial, power-of-sale foreclosure under a deed of trust involves no lawsuit and no judge; it proceeds entirely through the recorded notices and statutory waiting periods described in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "a power of sale is conferred upon the mortgagee, trustee, or any other person, to be exercised after a breach of the obligation for which that mortgage or transfer is a security"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.&lawCode=CIV)
  "made pursuant to an order, judgment, or decree of a court of record"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause quotes a single passage from Civil Code § 2924(a) that itself frames the power-of-sale mechanism and, in the same sentence, distinguishes it from a transfer made pursuant to a court order, judgment, or decree — that definitional contrast is drawn directly from the statute's own text and independently verified. Separately, the widely repeated practitioner claim that most California residential mortgage lenders specifically choose a deed of trust with a power-of-sale clause, rather than a mortgage without one, because it enables this faster nonjudicial process, was not independently verified against a primary source to the same standard as the statutory quotes in this document — it is not stated as fact in this clause, and no such claim is made or relied on here beyond the statute's own text.

WHO MAY RECORD A NOTICE OF DEFAULT
California Civil Code § 2924(a)(1) identifies who may record a notice of default: "The trustee, mortgagee, or beneficiary, or any of their authorized agents" — meaning the loan's beneficiary, the trustee under the deed of trust, or an authorized agent of either. Section 2924(a)(6) narrows that further: "An entity shall not record or cause a notice of default to be recorded or otherwise initiate the foreclosure process unless it is the holder of the beneficial interest under the mortgage or deed of trust, the original trustee or the substituted trustee under the deed of trust, or the designated agent of the holder of the beneficial interest." For the loan encumbering 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, the beneficiary named is Example Mortgage Lending, Inc., and the trustee named, if known, is Statewide Trustee Services, Inc.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The trustee, mortgagee, or beneficiary, or any of their authorized agents"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.&lawCode=CIV)
  "An entity shall not record or cause a notice of default to be recorded or otherwise initiate the foreclosure process unless it is the holder of the beneficial interest under the mortgage or deed of trust, the original trustee or the substituted trustee under the deed of trust, or the designated agent of the holder of the beneficial interest."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2924(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 2924(a)(6) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2924.&lawCode=CIV)

This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section — Civil Code § 2924(a)(1) (who may generally file a notice of default) and § 2924(a)(6) (the narrower restriction on who may actually record one or otherwise initiate foreclosure) — quoted together because the second subsection qualifies and narrows the first.

NOTICE OF DEFAULT — STATUTORY TRIGGER AND REQUIRED CONTENT
Before a trustee's sale of 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 can occur under a power of sale, California Civil Code § 2924(a)(1) requires that "The trustee, mortgagee, or beneficiary, or any of their authorized agents shall first file for record, in the office of the recorder of each county wherein the mortgaged or trust property or some part or parcel thereof is situated, a notice of default." If a Notice of Default affecting 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: August 1, 2026. By statute, that recorded notice of default must include: (A) "A statement identifying the mortgage or deed of trust by stating the name or names of the trustor or trustors and giving the book and page, or instrument number, if applicable, where the mortgage or deed of trust is recorded or a description of the mortgaged or trust property"; (B) "A statement that a breach of the obligation for which the mortgage or transfer in trust is security has occurred"; (C) "A statement setting forth the nature of each breach actually known to the beneficiary and of the beneficiary’s election to sell or cause to be sold the property to satisfy that obligation and any other obligation secured by the deed of trust or mortgage that is in default"; and (D), where the default is curable, a statement of the borrower's reinstatement rights under Section 2924c. If an amount has been stated as in default for this loan, it is stated as: $14,250.00.

All five quoted passages in this clause are drawn from a single statutory paragraph, Civil Code § 2924(a)(1), and its four lettered subparagraphs (A) through (D) — they are quoted together, rather than in separate clauses, because they jointly define the single statutory content requirement for one document (the notice of default), not because they are unrelated provisions being combined.

MINIMUM WAITING PERIOD BETWEEN NOTICE OF DEFAULT AND NOTICE OF SALE
After a notice of default affecting 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is recorded, California Civil Code § 2924(a)(2) requires that "Not less than three months shall elapse from the filing of the notice of default" before a notice of sale may be given. Section 2924(a)(3) then ties the next statutory step to that waiting period: "after the lapse of the three months described in paragraph (2), the mortgagee, trustee, or other person authorized to take the sale shall give notice of sale, stating the time and place thereof, in the manner and for a time not less than that set forth in Section 2924f." A limited exception in Section 2924(a)(4) permits a notice of sale to be recorded up to five days before the three-month period lapses, provided the sale date itself is set no earlier than three months and 20 days after the notice of default was recorded.

NOTICE OF SALE — MINIMUM TIMING, POSTING, AND PUBLICATION REQUIREMENTS
California Civil Code § 2924f governs the notice of sale that follows a notice of default. Before a trustee's sale of 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 can occur, "notice of the sale thereof shall be given by posting a written notice of the time of sale and of the street address and the specific place at the street address where the sale will be held, and describing the property to be sold, at least 20 days before the date of sale in one public place in the city where the property is to be sold, if the property is to be sold in a city, or, if not, then in one public place in the county seat of the county where the property is to be sold, and publishing a copy once a week for three consecutive calendar weeks." The statute further requires that "[t]he first publication [be] at least 20 days before the date of sale, in a newspaper of general circulation published in the public notice district in which the property or some part thereof is situated"; that "A copy of the notice of sale shall also be posted in a conspicuous place on the property to be sold at least 20 days before the date of sale, where possible and where not restricted for any reason"; and that the notice of sale "be recorded with the county recorder of the county in which the property or some part thereof is situated at least 20 days prior to the date of sale."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

This clause cites four different paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision — Civil Code § 2924f(b)(1) through (b)(4) — each addressing a distinct minimum-20-day requirement (posting in a public place, first newspaper publication, posting on the property itself, and recording with the county recorder), quoted together because they are the four components of one statutory notice-of-sale requirement. This document does not address subdivisions (c) through (f) of Section 2924f, which cover narrower topics such as owner-occupied single-family residences purchased under installment sales contracts, tenant purchase-agreement postponement rights, and minimum-bid fair market value requirements.

RIGHT TO REINSTATE THE LOAN BY CURING THE DEFAULT
California Civil Code § 2924c gives the trustor and certain other interested parties a statutory right to cure a default and reinstate the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 — without paying the full loan balance. The trustor or mortgagor, their successor in interest, or certain subordinate lienholders "may pay to the beneficiary or the mortgagee or their successors in interest, respectively, the entire amount due, at the time payment is tendered, with respect to (A) all amounts of principal, interest, taxes, assessments, insurance premiums, or advances actually known by the beneficiary to be, and that are, in default and shown in the notice of default, under the terms of the deed of trust or mortgage and the obligation secured thereby, (B) all amounts in default on recurring obligations not shown in the notice of default, and (C) all reasonable costs and expenses, subject to subdivision (c), that are actually incurred, or will be incurred as a direct result of the payment being tendered, in enforcing the terms of the obligation, deed of trust, or mortgage, and trustee's or attorney's fees, subject to subdivision (d), other than the portion of principal as would not then be due had no default occurred, and thereby cure the default theretofore existing, and thereupon, all proceedings theretofore had or instituted shall be dismissed or discontinued and the obligation and deed of trust or mortgage shall be reinstated and shall be and remain in force and effect, the same as if the acceleration had not occurred." As to timing, Section 2924c(e) provides that "[r]einstatement of a monetary default under the terms of an obligation secured by a deed of trust, or mortgage may be made at any time within the period commencing with the date of recordation of the notice of default until five business days prior to the date of sale set forth in the initial recorded notice of sale. In the event the sale does not take place on the date set forth in the initial recorded notice of sale or a subsequent recorded notice of sale is required to be given, the right of reinstatement shall be revived as of the date of recordation of the subsequent notice of sale."

ANTI-DEFICIENCY PROTECTION AFTER A NONJUDICIAL (POWER-OF-SALE) FORECLOSURE SALE
California Code of Civil Procedure § 580d provides a distinct consumer-protection rule specific to nonjudicial, power-of-sale foreclosure sales: "Except as provided in subdivision (b), no deficiency shall be owed or collected, and no deficiency judgment shall be rendered for a deficiency on a note secured by a deed of trust or mortgage on real property or an estate for years therein executed in any case in which the real property or estate for years therein has been sold by the mortgagee or trustee under power of sale contained in the mortgage or deed of trust." In other words, if 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is sold at a nonjudicial trustee's sale for less than the amount owed on the loan, Example Mortgage Lending, Inc. may not obtain a court judgment against Pat Morgan for that shortfall on the note secured by the deed of trust. The statute carves out one express limit on that protection: "[t]he fact that no deficiency shall be owed or collected under the circumstances set forth in subdivision (a) does not affect the liability that a guarantor, pledgor, or other surety might otherwise have with respect to the deficiency, or that might otherwise be satisfied in whole or in part from other collateral pledged to secure the obligation that is the subject of the deficiency."

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 580d(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 580d(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=580d.&lawCode=CCP)

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 580d(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 580d(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=580d.&lawCode=CCP)

expectedJSON.body: California Civil Code § 2924c gives the trustor and certain other interested parties a statutory right to cure a default and reinstate the loan secured by 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 — without paying the full loan balance. The trustor or mortgagor, their successor in interest, or certain subordinate lienholders "may pay to the beneficiary or the mortgagee or their successors in interest, respectively, the entire amount due, at the time payment is tendered, with respect to (A) all amounts of principal, interest, taxes, assessments, insurance premiums, or advances actually known by the beneficiary to be, and that are, in default and shown in the notice of default, under the terms of the deed of trust or mortgage and the obligation secured thereby, (B) all amounts in default on recurring obligations not shown in the notice of default, and (C) all reasonable costs and expenses, subject to subdivision (c), that are actually incurred, or will be incurred as a direct result of the payment being tendered, in enforcing the terms of the obligation, deed of trust, or mortgage, and trustee's or attorney's fees, subject to subdivision (d), other than the portion of principal as would not then be due had no default occurred, and thereby cure the default theretofore existing, and thereupon, all proceedings theretofore had or instituted shall be dismissed or discontinued and the obligation and deed of trust or mortgage shall be reinstated and shall be and remain in force and effect, the same as if the acceleration had not occurred." As to timing, Section 2924c(e) provides that "[r]einstatement of a monetary default under the terms of an obligation secured by a deed of trust, or mortgage may be made at any time within the period commencing with the date of recordation of the notice of default until five business days prior to the date of sale set forth in the initial recorded notice of sale. In the event the sale does not take place on the date set forth in the initial recorded notice of sale or a subsequent recorded notice of sale is required to be given, the right of reinstatement shall be revived as of the date of recordation of the subsequent notice of sale."

expectedJSON.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 580d provides a distinct consumer-protection rule specific to nonjudicial, power-of-sale foreclosure sales: "Except as provided in subdivision (b), no deficiency shall be owed or collected, and no deficiency judgment shall be rendered for a deficiency on a note secured by a deed of trust or mortgage on real property or an estate for years therein executed in any case in which the real property or estate for years therein has been sold by the mortgagee or trustee under power of sale contained in the mortgage or deed of trust." In other words, if 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is sold at a nonjudicial trustee's sale for less than the amount owed on the loan, Example Mortgage Lending, Inc. may not obtain a court judgment against Pat Morgan for that shortfall on the note secured by the deed of trust. The statute carves out one express limit on that protection: "[t]he fact that no deficiency shall be owed or collected under the circumstances set forth in subdivision (a) does not affect the liability that a guarantor, pledgor, or other surety might otherwise have with respect to the deficiency, or that might otherwise be satisfied in whole or in part from other collateral pledged to secure the obligation that is the subject of the deficiency."
